records.name: A drug makes people live longer in good health

missing.what: The three-drug healthspan trial led from San Antonio (VITAL-H, paid for by the United States agency ARPA-H) now has a registry entry, NCT07923630, first posted on 2026-11-06. The entry lists it as not yet recruiting, with an estimated 1,200 people aged 60 to 75, a start in January 2027, 36 months of treatment and main results expected in December 2030. It names two drugs against placebo, dapagliflozin and semaglutide in pill form; rapamycin, which the university's release of 2026-03-04 and the agency's announcement of 2026-02-24 named as a third drug, is not in the registry entry, and the 726 people of the release has become 1,200. Its main measure is a score of physical performance (balance, walking speed and rising from a chair), not time to disease or death. The weekly readings in data/scans mention this trial (726 adults, awaiting ethics approval) but hold no registry number; the treatment's own entry does not mention the trial at all.
missing.why: It is the first registered, funded, placebo-controlled trial of approved drugs with ageing itself as the purpose, and it is due to read out around 2031, the entry's earliest year for the first-human rung. But its main measure is physical function over three years, not longer life or longer freedom from age-related disease, so on a plain reading a positive result would not meet the test; it bears on the estimate's reasoning (which names only the metformin trial) more than on the years.

missing.what: The United States agency ARPA-H announced seven teams in its PROSPR programme, with up to 144 million dollars over five years, to test treatments meant to add healthy years. The teams include the University of Texas Health Science Center at San Antonio (a trial of approved drugs: an SGLT2 inhibitor, rapamycin and semaglutide) and the company Cambrian BioPharma (a new relative of rapamycin taken daily). The university's own release of 2026-03-04 gives its share as up to 38 million dollars and says enrolment starts in 2027. The entry's estimate reasons only from the unfunded metformin trial and does not mention that public money for trials of this kind now exists.
missing.why: The estimate's likely year assumes a trial 'of metformin or a successor' starts by 2029; a government-funded set of trials starting in 2027 makes that start more likely than the entry's wording allows. These trials measure function over a few years, so they bear on the reasoning and on the entry about a regulator accepting a marker more than on this entry's test.

missing.what: A study of United States transplant registry records in the journal GeroScience (Stewart and Fitzsimmons) compared 4,885 kidney transplant recipients prescribed rapamycin with 6,589 who were not, followed for a median of 11 years. After adjustment the median age at death was 64.6 years with rapamycin and 64.3 without, a difference the authors call statistically similar (95 per cent interval minus 1.6 to plus 2.0 years); they report no meaningful gain in long-term survival. Not found anywhere in data/.
missing.why: It is a study of records in sick people on transplant doses, not a controlled trial in healthy people, so it cannot meet or fail the test. It is the largest published look at long exposure to rapamycin and survival in people and it found nothing, which weighs a little against the hope the description names.

checked: Harrison and colleagues, Nature, 2009-07-08 (https://doi.org/10.1038/nature08221): abstract read in Europe PMC; rapamycin fed from 600 days of age (about 20 months) lengthened life in male and female mice; the entry is right.

PEARL rapamycin trial (Moel and colleagues, Aging, 2025-04-04, https://doi.org/10.18632/aging.206235): published in April 2025 as the entry says; its registry entry NCT04488601 is listed as completed with 129 enrolled and no results posted on the registry.
The metformin trial (TAME): searches of ClinicalTrials.gov on 2026-11-09 by title, by short name and by sponsor still return no entry for it, as the entry says.

The sponsor's page https://www.afar.org/tame-trial still answers 'not found' on 2026-11-09, as the entry says; a second address a search engine offered (https://www.afar.org/research/TAME/) also answers 'not found'.
queries: ClinicalTrials.gov: Targeting Aging with Metformin; TAME metformin aging; American Federation for Aging Research; metformin AND aging AND (multimorbidity OR healthspan OR longevity); healthspan AND (dapagliflozin OR rapamycin OR semaglutide) AND older adults; rapamycin AND (aging OR ageing OR healthspan OR longevity); VITAL-H; PROSPR ARPA-H; Barshop healthspan

Europe PMC from 2025-01-01: TITLE:rapamycin AND TITLE:(lifespan OR healthspan OR longevity) AND (marmoset OR primate OR humans OR randomized); TITLE:(geroprotect* OR gerotherapeutic*) AND TITLE:(trial OR randomized OR randomised); rapamycin AND marmoset AND (lifespan OR survival) from 2024-01-01

Web: TAME trial metformin aging funding launch 2026; ARPA-H healthspan trial rapamycin dapagliflozin semaglutide San Antonio 726 adults enrolment; rapamycin marmoset lifespan study results Salmon; ARPA-H PROSPR awardees announced healthspan trials 2026; 'Targeting Aging with Metformin' OR 'TAME trial' AFAR announcement funding secured OR enrolling (limited to afar.org, the three release wires, statnews.com, nih.gov)
records.could_not_check: A reported result that rapamycin lengthened the lives of marmosets (said in public radio interviews in 2024 and 2025 by the San Antonio group) was seen only in a search summary; no paper or preprint with the survival figures turned up in Europe PMC, so it is not reported as a fact. The GeroScience paper was read as its abstract in Europe PMC, not the full text. Regulators outside the United States were covered only by web search, which returned no approval of any drug to slow ageing.

records.name: A drug is approved to make dogs live longer

corrections.entry_says: The pivotal trial (STAY) has 'about 1,000 to 1,300 dogs at 55 to 70 clinics'.
corrections.source_says: The company's post of 2025-07-14 says enrolment finished with 1,300 dogs at 72 veterinary clinics ('70+ clinics'), from more than 1,500 screened; its release of 2026-01-13 says about 1,300 dogs at 70 clinics, enrolment completed in July 2025. The range in the entry dates from before enrolment closed.

corrections.entry_says: Loyal has given the drug 'to 48 in a three-month pilot'.
corrections.source_says: Not confirmed. The company's own post on the pilot (2023) says the pilot met its enrolment goal of 60 dogs; that figure was seen in a search summary only, and no page opened gives 48. The company's brief for veterinarians, which describes the three-month pilot, could not be read (a file the tools could not turn into text). The number should be checked against its source before it stays.

missing.what: Loyal announced that its pivotal trial of the senior-dog drug (STAY) had finished enrolling: 1,300 dogs at 72 clinics. The entry gives the first dog dosed (December 2023) and a planned size, but not that enrolment closed in July 2025. Not found elsewhere in data/.
missing.why: It dates the trial that would supply the peer-reviewed report for the first rung: with enrolment closed in mid-2025 and a stated length of about four years, a read-out before about 2029 is unlikely. It does not bear on the conditional approval, which does not wait for this trial.

missing.what: Loyal announced a 100 million dollar funding round, led by the investment firm age1, and said it had completed two of the three major requirements for conditional approval of the senior-dog drug, with the money to pay for the final regulatory work and preparation for sale. The weekly reading of 2026-10-25 in data/scans saw this release for its statement on the sections; neither it nor the entry records the money.
missing.why: The estimate's latest year (2032) leans on 'the company running short of money, which in a company with one product family is a real risk'. A round of this size nine months ago makes that risk smaller for the next few years; it does not change the company's own timetable, so the likely year stands.

missing.what: The design of a second trial that measures lifespan in dogs was published in GeroScience: the Test of Rapamycin in Aging Dogs (TRIAD), a placebo-controlled trial of rapamycin in healthy middle-aged pet dogs run by the university-led Dog Aging Project, with lifespan as a stated measure. The publications log mentions the trial inside a 2022 paper's record (creevy-2022); the entry itself names only Loyal ('One company, Loyal ...') and does not say that a non-company trial could also supply the first rung.
missing.why: It is a design paper with no result, so it meets nothing. It matters because the entry's first rung ('a peer-reviewed report that dogs given such a drug lived longer') could be reached by this trial of an unapproved use of an existing drug, with no approval following, and the entry reads as if Loyal were the only route.

checked: United States veterinary regulator's list of announcements (https://www.fda.gov/animal-veterinary/news-events/cvm-updates), read 2026-11-09: it now runs to 2026-11-03. Nothing since 2026-09-30 is an approval or conditional approval of a drug to extend dogs' lives (the new items are an emergency authorisation for screwworm in dogs on 2026-11-03 and an approval of a skin-infection injection on 2026-10-20). The entry's statement that no approval exists still holds.

Acceptance of effectiveness for the senior-dog drug on 2025-02-26, with the company then expecting the manufacturing and safety sections by the end of 2025: confirmed on the company's post (https://loyal.com/posts/loy-002-rxe), which also gives first dog dosed in December 2023 and a trial of about four years.

Acceptance of the safety section announced 2026-01-13, with field data from over 400 dogs, and the sentence that the company 'expects to complete the final major technical section and apply for XCA next year': confirmed on the company's post (https://loyal.com/posts/loy-002-tas-announcement).
Acceptance of effectiveness for the second large-dog drug (LOY-003) announced on 2026-09-16: confirmed by Longevity.Technology's article of 2026-09-22.

The company's page for veterinarians (https://loyal.com/for-vets), read 2026-11-09: manufacturing 'In progress', conditional approval 'In progress', effectiveness and safety sections complete, as the entry says. The page dates the safety package to December 2025; the entry's 2026-01-13 is the date of the announcement.
queries: Europe PMC from 2023-01-01: LOY-002 OR LOY-001 OR LOY-003 OR (Loyal AND (canine OR dogs) AND lifespan); from 2024-01-01: TITLE:(dogs OR canine OR 'companion dogs') AND TITLE:(rapamycin OR lifespan OR longevity OR healthspan) AND (trial OR randomized OR placebo)

Web: Loyal LOY-002 FDA conditional approval manufacturing section 2026; Loyal dog longevity LOY-003 reasonable expectation of effectiveness FDA accepted; Loyal STAY study fully enrolled dogs clinics LOY-002 press release (limited to the release wires, loyal.com, dvm360.com, avma.org); Loyal LOY-002 pilot study 48 dogs three months; Dog Aging Project TRIAD rapamycin trial results OR enrollment complete 2026
ClinicalTrials.gov does not register veterinary trials, so no registry query applies.
records.could_not_check: The Business Wire copy of the 2026-02-11 release refused the fetch (the company's own post of the same day was read instead). One search summary gave 2026-08-17 as the date of a Business Wire release on LOY-003, against the 2026-09-16 the entry and Longevity.Technology give; the release itself was not opened, so the earlier date is unconfirmed. The size of the three-month pilot (48 in the entry) could not be confirmed either way. No peer-reviewed report of Loyal's own effectiveness data turned up in Europe PMC. The state of the Dog Aging Project's rapamycin trial in 2026 (enrolment, end date) was seen only in search summaries of weak sites and is not reported. Regulators outside the United States were covered by web search only; nothing was returned.

records.name: A drug that renews the cell's power plants improves muscle in older people

corrections.entry_says: 'four weeks of the compound in sixty healthy older adults was safe and switched on the mitochondrial genes in their muscle' (the 2019 report that the stage rests on).
corrections.source_says: The registry entry for that trial (NCT02655393) lists 60 people in all, split between single-dose groups and 28-day groups of 12 people each; only the 28-day groups had four weeks of the compound, so the four-week finding comes from a part of the sixty, not all of them. The registry and the paper's abstract both give safety as the main measure; the change in muscle genes was a secondary measure.

corrections.entry_says: 'a later controlled trial in older adults found modest gains in muscle endurance, and one in middle-aged adults gains in muscle strength.'
corrections.source_says: Both trials missed their pre-stated main measures, which the entry does not say. In the older-adults trial (Liu and colleagues, JAMA Network Open, 2022-01-04; 66 people) the main measures were six-minute walking distance and the muscle's peak energy output, and the paper says the gains on both 'were not significant for urolithin A'; endurance was a secondary measure. In the middle-aged trial (Singh and colleagues, Cell Reports Medicine, 2022-05) the abstract says there was no significant improvement on peak power output, the main measure; strength was a secondary measure.

corrections.entry_says: Stage 'first-human', reached 2019-06-14, against a test that asks for a controlled trial in which the drug 'improves muscle strength, endurance or walking more than placebo on the trial's pre-stated main measure'.
corrections.source_says: On a plain reading no report the entry cites meets those words: the 2019 trial's main measure was safety, and the two 2022 trials missed their main measures (see above). The registry shows the maker calls its next muscle-strength trial 'confirmatory' (NCT07231783, 120 middle-aged adults, results due after October 2027). Either the stage or the test's wording for the first-human rung needs a look.

corrections.entry_says: 'The approval of such a drug for a rare inherited disease in 2025, if confirmed, means the regulatory path exists'.
corrections.source_says: It is confirmed, with a qualification the entry lacks. On 2025-09-19 the United States Food and Drug Administration granted accelerated approval to elamipretide (sold as Forzinity, Stealth BioTherapeutics) for Barth syndrome in patients weighing at least 30 kg, on the strength of improved strength in one leg muscle; the regulator requires a further placebo-controlled trial to confirm that the gain helps patients. It is an accelerated approval, not a full one.

missing.what: The United States regulator's own announcement of the accelerated approval of elamipretide for Barth syndrome, a rare inherited disease of the mitochondria. The entry refers to this approval without the date, the drug, the company or the regulator, and with 'if confirmed'. Not found elsewhere in data/ (the weekly reading of 2026-11-08 searched on the drug's name but logged no approval).
missing.why: Barth syndrome is an inherited disease of children and young adults, not an age-related condition, so the clinic test ('a regulator approves such a drug for an age-related condition') is not met. The estimate already assumes this approval; confirming it removes the doubt but does not move the years.

missing.what: The same drug is in a late-stage trial for an age-related condition, which the entry does not mention. The registry lists the ReNEW trial of elamipretide in dry age-related macular degeneration (NCT06373731) as fully enrolled with 313 people aged 55 and over, 96 weeks of treatment, the main measure at week 48, and main results expected in August 2027 (entry last updated 2026-09-17). A review of the approval in the journal Drugs (2025-12-03) confirms the drug is in late-stage development for that eye condition.
missing.why: The clinic test asks only that a regulator approve 'such a drug for an age-related condition'; an approval for this eye condition would meet those words even though the entry is about muscle. A read-out in 2027 makes the entry's earliest year (2031) reachable by a route the estimate's reasons do not name, and whether an eye approval should count is a question for the entry's owner.

missing.what: The maker of urolithin A registered a trial it titles 'confirmatory': 120 healthy adults aged 40 to 65, two doses against placebo for six months, with knee strength as the pre-stated main measure (NCT07231783, first posted 2025-11-17, recruiting, main results expected October 2027). It is registered as a trial of a dietary supplement, not a drug.
missing.why: This is the trial that could meet the first-human test as worded (a gain on the pre-stated main measure), and it has no result yet. It is in middle-aged adults and run as a supplement study, which supports the estimate's latest-case reasoning that the supplement route keeps the molecule out of drug trials.

missing.what: A placebo-controlled trial of urolithin A in frail older adults is listed as completed with no results posted: 26 people aged 65 to 85, eight weeks, main measures taken from muscle samples (NCT06556706, Amazentis; completed 2025-04-25, entry last updated 2025-05-28). No paper from it turned up in Europe PMC.
missing.why: It is the only completed trial in the frail older people the entry is about, and eighteen months on it has not reported. Its main measures are of the muscle's mitochondria, not of strength or walking, so it could not meet the test even if positive.

missing.what: A placebo-controlled trial of urolithin A in Nature Aging (Denk and colleagues): 50 healthy middle-aged adults, four weeks, main measures in immune cells, which changed in the direction hoped for. It is a controlled human result for this compound on a pre-stated main measure, but on the immune system, not muscle.
missing.why: The test names muscle strength, endurance or walking, so an immune result does not meet it. It makes the description's account of the human evidence incomplete.

missing.what: A placebo-controlled trial of urolithin A in JAMA Network Open (Pinaffi-Langley and colleagues, University of Oklahoma): 50 adults aged 40 to 64 with obesity, four weeks. The main measure, a test of how well an arm artery widens, did not differ from placebo. Registry entry NCT05921266.
missing.why: It is a third controlled trial of the compound to miss its main measure, after the two muscle trials of 2022. It is on blood vessels, not muscle, so it bears only on how likely a positive muscle trial around 2032 is.

missing.what: A first trial of elamipretide in ordinary older adults was registered: 30 people aged 65 to 80, daily for four weeks, with no placebo group and safety as the main measure (NCT07275424, University of Washington investigator, first posted 2025-12-10, recruiting).
missing.why: It shows the approved drug being tried in healthy ageing, which is the route the estimate's earliest year assumes. It is small and uncontrolled, so it can neither meet the test nor move a year.

checked: Andreux and colleagues, Nature Metabolism, 2019-06-14 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s42255-019-0073-4): date, first-in-human status, four-week dosing and the change in muscle mitochondrial genes confirmed from the abstract in Europe PMC; the number sixty confirmed as the trial's total from the registry.

Registry entries of the two 2022 trials: NCT03283462 (66 people aged 65 to 90, completed, no results posted on the registry) and NCT03464500 (90 people aged 40 to 65, completed, no results posted on the registry); both agree with the papers.
No regulator has approved urolithin A as a drug: nothing found to the contrary in the registry, Europe PMC or web searches.
queries: ClinicalTrials.gov: urolithin A (all 64 entries listed); elamipretide (all 21 entries listed)

Europe PMC: TITLE:'urolithin A' AND (randomized OR randomised OR placebo OR trial), trial reports and preprints from 2022-01-01; TITLE:(elamipretide) AND (trial OR approval OR randomized) from 2025-01-01; TITLE:(sarcopenia) AND TITLE:(mitochondri* OR mitophagy), randomised trials from 2025-01-01 (none)
Web: FDA grants accelerated approval elamipretide Forzinity Barth syndrome September 2025; Stealth BioTherapeutics elamipretide dry age-related macular degeneration phase 3 ReNEW ReGAIN results 2026
records.could_not_check: The full text of the 2019 Nature Metabolism paper sits behind a sign-in, so the exact number of people who had four weeks of the compound was not read from the paper; the registry shows 28-day groups of 12 people each and a total of 60. The Singh 2022 paper was read as its abstract only. No results of the late-stage eye trial have been announced as far as a web search shows; company releases were seen in search summaries only. Regulators outside the United States were not searched one by one. Drugs for age-related muscle loss that do not act on mitochondria were outside this entry's kind and were not searched.

records.name: A weight-loss drug is approved to prevent heart attacks and strokes in people without diabetes

corrections.entry_says: 'six months after Medicare plans began covering it only 32,732 prescriptions had been filled, under 1 per cent of an estimated 3.6 million eligible beneficiaries.'
corrections.source_says: 32,732 is the count for one month, September 2024, not a total for the six months. The paper's results give Medicare fills of Wegovy rising from 4,689 in February 2024 to 32,732 in September 2024; its discussion then sets that September figure against the estimated 3.6 million. The site's own publications log (scannell-2026) has it right; the entry's wording reads as a six-month total.

corrections.entry_says: 'the first published uptake figure for the heart-prevention purpose is a study in the American Journal of Managed Care (Scannell and colleagues, 2026-07-09)'; the estimate note calls it 'the record's one published uptake figure'.
corrections.source_says: Earlier published uptake figures for this purpose exist. A study in the European Heart Journal's quality-of-care journal (Chi and colleagues), published online 2025-09-02, used health records of 298,344 people with obesity and heart disease but no diabetes, mostly in the United States, to 2025-05-06: 3.4 per cent started one of these drugs over the whole period, and the yearly rate rose from 1.2 per cent before the trial result to 2.5 per cent after it. A research letter in JACC: Advances (Do and colleagues, 2026-01-22) on dispensing after the 2024 approval also predates it (title seen, text not opened).

corrections.entry_says: The trial 'cut heart attacks, strokes and heart deaths by a fifth over three years'.
corrections.source_says: Right in substance. The paper gives 17,604 people, events in 6.5 per cent on the drug against 8.0 per cent on placebo (hazard ratio 0.80) over a mean follow-up of 39.8 months, which is a little over three years. No change needed; noted for exactness.

missing.what: Britain's medicines regulator (the MHRA) authorised semaglutide (Wegovy) to lower the risk of heart death, heart attack and stroke in adults with established heart disease who are overweight or obese. The entry records only the United States approval. Not found in data/.
missing.why: For wide use: 'available by prescription for that purpose in several countries and taken by a substantial share of eligible people'. A second regulator's approval goes to the first half of those words (several countries); it says nothing on the second half (a substantial share of eligible people), which the uptake studies say is not met. So the wide-use test is not met, but the entry understates how far the approval has spread.

missing.what: The European Medicines Agency's committee gave a positive opinion on adding the same heart-protection wording to Wegovy's European label, for adults with established heart disease and a body-mass index of 27 or more without diabetes (reported 2024-07-26 by Pharmaceutical Technology, which described the change as not yet final). Australia's regulator has also approved the drug for people with overweight or obesity and established heart disease: a study in the Medical Journal of Australia of 2026-08-01 counts up to 338,900 Australian adults who meet that approved use. Neither is in the entry or elsewhere in data/.
missing.why: With the United States, Britain, the European Union and Australia, the 'several countries' part of the wide-use test looks met on a plain reading. The 'substantial share of eligible people' part is not, on every uptake figure found. The European Commission's final decision and its date were not opened.

missing.what: A study of health records (Chi and colleagues, European Heart Journal - Quality of Care and Clinical Outcomes; online 2025-09-02, in print May 2026) of 298,344 people with obesity and heart disease but no diabetes, from 148 health organisations (70 of them, with most of the patients, in the United States), to 2025-05-06. 3.4 per cent started one of these drugs over the whole period; the yearly rate was 1.2 per cent before the heart trial reported and 2.5 per cent after; about 1 per cent of those aged 75 or over started. Not in data/.
missing.why: It is a second, independent uptake figure for exactly the people the approval covers, with data eight months later than the one the entry holds, and it also shows a few per cent a year. That supports the later years (2030 earliest, 2033 likely) set on 2026-10-17 and shows the test's 'substantial share' was not met by mid-2025.

missing.what: The United States regulator approved a pill form of semaglutide (the Wegovy pill, 25 mg daily) for weight loss and to reduce the risk of major heart events, as reported by the American Journal of Managed Care on the day, citing the maker's release. A research letter in Annals of Internal Medicine of 2026-10-13 (Jelwan and colleagues) reports on early uptake of the pill (title seen only). The entry's estimate says 'prices were falling as pills and copies arrived' but records neither the pill's approval nor that its label carries the heart purpose. Not in data/.
missing.why: A pill approved for the same heart-protection purpose removes the injection as a barrier and is cheaper to make, which bears on how fast a substantial share of eligible people could be reached. It is an approval of a second form of the same drug, not a new stage.

missing.what: Medicare began a temporary programme (the Medicare GLP-1 Bridge) under which eligible people on its drug plans can get certain of these drugs for a 50 dollar monthly payment, from 2026-07-01 to 2027-12-31 (the programme's own page, last updated 2026-07-13). The entry's uptake figure dates from 2024, when Medicare paid for Wegovy only for the heart purpose and take-up was under 1 per cent. Not in data/.
missing.why: The low Medicare figure is the main reason the wide-use years were moved later on 2026-10-17. A capped monthly cost for older Americans from mid-2026 changes the payer conditions behind that figure, so the next uptake numbers may be much higher; the programme is temporary and its page does not name the drugs or the eligibility rules, so the size of the effect is unknown.

missing.what: Copies of semaglutide have begun to reach the market outside the United States and Europe: a web search reports Health Canada's approval of a first copy on 2026-04-28 with a launch in May 2026, and patents ending in India (2026-03-20, followed by dozens of brands), China and Brazil in 2026. Seen in search summaries only; no regulator's page was opened.
missing.why: The estimate's reasons mention copies arriving but give no fact. If confirmed, cheaper copies in several large countries make a substantial share of eligible people more reachable there, though mostly under diabetes labels rather than the heart-protection purpose this entry tracks.

checked: Lincoff and colleagues, New England Journal of Medicine, 2023-11-11 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2307563): 17,604 people, no diabetes, hazard ratio 0.80; the entry is right.

Scannell and colleagues, American Journal of Managed Care, 2026-07-09: date, authors, the 136.4 per cent rise (367,371 fills in February 2024 to 868,301 in September 2024), 32,732 and 3.6 million all confirmed on the journal's page (see the correction on how 32,732 is worded).
Feng and colleagues, Nature, 2026-09-02 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-026-10940-7): date, 20-month-old female mice and longer life confirmed from the abstract.
The weekly readings' note that tirzepatide was approved on 2026-08-28 to cut heart events in adults with type 2 diabetes is outside this entry's test (people with diabetes) and was not re-checked.
queries: Europe PMC from 2024-03-08: TITLE:(semaglutide OR wegovy OR 'GLP-1') AND TITLE:(uptake OR utilization OR utilisation OR prescribing OR eligibility OR eligible OR dispensing) AND (cardiovascular OR SELECT) AND (overweight OR obesity) (51 results read by title); TITLE:(semaglutide OR tirzepatide OR orforglipron OR retatrutide) AND TITLE:('cardiovascular outcomes' OR 'all-cause mortality' OR 'major adverse cardiovascular') AND (without diabetes OR obesity), randomised trials

Web: Wegovy cardiovascular risk reduction indication approved EMA CHMP MHRA Health Canada TGA label update; FDA approves oral Wegovy pill semaglutide 25 mg reduce risk major adverse cardiovascular events; MHRA approves Wegovy semaglutide prevent heart attack stroke gov.uk July 2024; Medicare coverage Wegovy Zepbound obesity 2026 GLP-1 bridge BALANCE model; generic semaglutide launch 2026 Canada India China Brazil patent expiry
The trial registry was not queried drug by drug for this entry: its stage is already past the trial rungs, and the next rung is settled by uptake figures and approvals.
pages_opened: Europe PMC abstracts: PMID 42604458 (Medical Journal of Australia), DOI 10.1038/s41586-026-10940-7, DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2307563
records.could_not_check: The JACC: Advances letter on dispensing after the approval (Do and colleagues, 2026-01-22, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacadv.2025.102575) refused the fetch and has no abstract in Europe PMC, so its figures are not reported. The same holds for the Annals of Internal Medicine letter on the pill's early uptake (https://doi.org/10.7326/annals-26-02436) and a JAMA letter on uptake of these drugs for obesity (2025-06-01, https://doi.org/10.1001/jama.2025.4735). The 742 and 834 days in the mouse paper are not in its abstract and were not checked. The European Commission's final decision on the label, Health Canada's and Japan's, China's and South Korea's positions on the heart-protection purpose were not opened. Which drugs and which people the Medicare programme covers was read only in search summaries (Wegovy in both forms, Zepbound and a newly approved pill named Foundayo). The United States regulator's own label for the pill was not opened; the indication is as a trade journal reported it.

records.name: A supplement that raises a cell's NAD improves an age-related function in a controlled trial

corrections.entry_says: The 2021 trial was in 'overweight women past the menopause'.
corrections.source_says: The paper's abstract and title say the women also had prediabetes (blood sugar above normal but short of diabetes): 'postmenopausal women with prediabetes who were overweight or obese'. The registry entry (NCT03151239) lists 25 people, a number the entry does not give. The registry confirms that muscle insulin response was the pre-stated main measure, so the stage record does meet the test as worded.

corrections.entry_says: 'Larger trials have been mixed' and 'The 2021 result is small and in one function; the treatment stays at first human until a larger trial.'
corrections.source_says: Larger trials have since reported, and the entry names none. The largest, in JAMA on 2026-10-08, found the compound did worse than placebo on its main measure; the same St Louis university's own larger repeat of the 2021 trial has posted results in which the main measure did not favour the compound (both under 'missing'). 'Mixed' now understates how the larger trials have gone.

missing.what: The largest controlled trial yet of an NAD-raising compound reported in JAMA (the NOPARK trial; Brakedal and colleagues, Haukeland University Hospital, Norway; registry entry NCT03568968). 410 people with early Parkinson's disease took nicotinamide riboside or placebo for a year. On the pre-stated main measure, a standard score of Parkinson's symptoms, those on the compound got worse by 2.45 points and those on placebo improved by 0.27, a difference of 2.72 points in favour of placebo (P = 0.02); a score of non-movement symptoms also worsened more on the compound. The authors conclude it did not improve outcomes and was associated with worse outcomes than placebo. Not found anywhere in data/, although it was published nine days before the weekly reading of 2026-10-17.
missing.why: Parkinson's is an age-related condition and this was the one late-stage trial of such a compound for one; a positive result was the most direct route to an approval. It failed and pointed the wrong way, which supports the estimate's latest case ('the mixed trials being the true answer') and argues for later years on the clinic rung. It does not undo the 2021 first-human result, which was on a different function.

missing.what: The St Louis university behind the 2021 result posted results of its own larger repeat on the registry (NCT04571008, Washington University): 56 overweight people aged 45 to 75 with prediabetes, NMN or placebo for at least 16 weeks, with the same main measure as the 2021 trial (muscle response to insulin). Twenty people in each group finished. The posted mean change in the main measure was 13.5 with NMN and 19.0 with placebo (standard deviations 88.4 and 95.0), so the compound's group did not improve more than placebo's. No paper from it turned up in Europe PMC. Not found in data/.
missing.why: The entry's stage rests on one trial of 25 women, and this is the same group's larger test of the same measure; on the posted numbers it did not repeat the finding. The registry gives no clear test of the difference (its one figure, 0.05, reads as the threshold, not a result), so this needs the paper before anyone leans on it, but it bears directly on how firm the first-human rung is.

missing.what: A controlled trial older than the entry and not in it (the NICE trial; McDermott and colleagues, Nature Communications; registry entry NCT03743636, results posted on the registry 2025-01-14): 90 people with narrowed leg arteries took nicotinamide riboside, with or without a second compound, or placebo for six months. On the pre-stated main measure, distance walked in six minutes, the compound alone beat placebo by 17.6 metres (plus 7.0 against minus 10.6 metres; the paper reports a one-sided 90 per cent interval starting at 1.8 metres). The same team has registered a larger repeat, 250 people aged 50 and over, due to start in December 2026 with main results in December 2030 (NCT07782671, first posted 2026-08-24). Not found in data/.
missing.why: On a plain reading it meets the first-human test a second time and in a larger trial: 'improves an age-related function (... walking) more than placebo on the trial's pre-stated main measure, in a peer-reviewed report'. The stage does not change, since the entry is already at first human, but the entry should name it, and the repeat due in 2030 is the academic trial the estimate's likely year (early 2030s) assumes without naming.

missing.what: A controlled pilot trial of nicotinamide riboside in older adults with mild memory impairment (Martens and colleagues, Alzheimer's & Dementia; 42 people finished, 12 weeks) found blood NAD doubled but no improvement in memory and thinking, its main measure. The weekly reading of 2026-10-18 noted this trial (it gives the date as 2026-07-21); the treatment's own entry does not mention it.
missing.why: One more controlled trial in older people that raised NAD and missed its main measure. It is small; it adds to the pattern rather than moving a year by itself.

missing.what: A controlled pilot trial in GeroScience (Lin and colleagues): 54 inactive adults aged 55 and over with raised blood pressure; six weeks of nicotinamide riboside with walking exercise lowered daytime blood pressure no more than placebo with the same exercise, its main measure. Not found in data/.
missing.why: Blood vessels are one of the functions the test names, and this controlled trial in older adults missed its main measure. Small, so it bears on the description's 'mixed' more than on the years.

missing.what: The United States Food and Drug Administration reversed its earlier position and concluded that NMN is not excluded from being sold as a dietary supplement, in answers to petitions from trade groups (reported by the trade paper Nutritional Outlook on 2025-09-30). The entry says both compounds 'are sold as supplements' and does not record that NMN's legal standing as one was in dispute until then, or that the regulator's reasoning turned on NMN having been authorised for study as a new drug. Not found in data/.
missing.why: It is a ruling about sale as a supplement, which the test excludes, so it meets nothing. It bears on the estimate's statement that no company was taking such a compound through drug trials: the regulator's letters confirm one had been authorised for study as a drug, and the registry shows a company (Metro International Biotech) with a completed mid-stage trial of a drug-grade NMN in 124 young adults (NCT05878119, no results posted).

checked: Yoshino and colleagues, Science, 2021-04-22 (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.abe9985): date, ten weeks, placebo control, improved muscle response to insulin all confirmed from the abstract; registry entry NCT03151239 is completed with 25 enrolled and muscle insulin response as the main measure.
No approval of either compound as a treatment by any regulator turned up in the registry, Europe PMC or web searches; the entry's statement stands.
queries: ClinicalTrials.gov: nicotinamide riboside (131 entries; those stopped, withdrawn, with results posted since 2025, completed since mid-2024, or with 150 or more people were read); nicotinamide mononucleotide OR NMN OR MIB-626 (63 entries, same filter)

Europe PMC from 2024-01-01: TITLE:('nicotinamide riboside' OR 'nicotinamide mononucleotide' OR NMN OR 'NAD+ precursor' OR 'NAD precursor' OR 'MIB-626' OR NOPARK), trial reports and preprints (29 results read by title)
Web: NOPARK trial results nicotinamide riboside Parkinson's disease phase 3; FDA NMN dietary supplement decision September 2025
pages_opened: Europe PMC abstracts: PMID 42848371 (JAMA, NOPARK), 38871717, 42478598, 40459998, 42009009, 40770531, and DOI 10.1126/science.abe9985
records.could_not_check: The JAMA paper and the others were read as abstracts in Europe PMC, not full texts. The entry's statement that the 2021 trial 'did not change their weight, blood sugar or fitness' is not in the abstract and was not checked. The regulator's own letters on NMN were not opened (a trade paper's report was). Trials in rare inherited diseases (a premature-ageing syndrome in Aging Cell on 2025-06-03; a nerve disease in Lancet Neurology on 2026-05-01) were seen and left out as not age-related conditions in ordinary older people. Three 2026 preprints from a supplement maker on injected nicotinamide riboside were seen by title only. Regulators outside the United States were not searched one by one.

records.name: Metformin delays age-related disease in people who do not have diabetes

corrections.entry_says: The entry is 'the clearest case on the site of a treatment that cannot reach the clinic rung because nobody will pay to find out', and its estimate reasons only from the unfunded TAME trial ('If the trial started in 2027 it would read out around 2034').
corrections.source_says: Two controlled trials of metformin against placebo in people without diabetes, with heart disease, cancer, dementia and death as measures, have been paid for by public bodies. One is running: the United States veterans' health service's VA-IMPACT trial (NCT02915198) is recruiting an estimated 7,410 people with prediabetes and artery disease, with death, heart attack and stroke as the main measure and main results expected in September 2029. The other has reported: the Diabetes Prevention Program gave metformin or placebo to people at high risk of diabetes from 1996 and has followed them for 21 years (see 'missing'). The statement that nobody will pay to find out holds for TAME's design, not for the question.

corrections.entry_says: 'in 2013 a National Institute on Aging group found that a low dose lengthened the lives of middle-aged mice by about six per cent.'
corrections.source_says: The paper's abstract says the low dose, started at middle age, extended healthspan and lifespan 'in male mice', and that a higher dose was toxic. The entry leaves out that the finding is in males only. The six per cent figure is not in the abstract and was not checked against the full text.

missing.what: A controlled trial has already tested metformin against placebo in people without diabetes for three of the outcomes the test names, and found no delay in two of them. The Diabetes Prevention Program assigned 3,234 adults at high risk of diabetes to metformin, placebo or a lifestyle programme from 1996 to 1999 and has followed them for a median of 21 years. Cancer (Cancer Prevention Research, 2025-07-01): 173 first cancers on metformin against 191 on placebo, hazard ratio 0.90 with a 95 per cent interval of 0.73 to 1.10, no reduction. Deaths (Diabetes Care, 2021-10-25): hazard ratio 0.99 for death from any cause. Heart attack, stroke and heart death (Circulation, 2022-05-23): hazard ratio 1.03. The authors note that many people in every group later took metformin outside the study, which may have blurred the comparison. None of these reports is in the entry or anywhere in data/.
missing.why: The test asks for 'A peer-reviewed, controlled trial in people without diabetes reports that those taking metformin reached a first age-related disease (heart disease, cancer, dementia) or death later than those on placebo'. This trial is that kind of trial (people without diabetes at the start, placebo control, peer-reviewed) and on cancer, heart events and death it found no delay, so the test is not met. It is the strongest human evidence there is on the entry's question and it points against a positive result, which argues for later years and should at least be named beside the medical-records studies the description cites.

missing.what: A preprint from the same trial reports on dementia (Wander and colleagues, medRxiv, 2026-08-07): being assigned to metformin was associated with 60 per cent lower odds of dementia than placebo (odds ratio 0.40, 95 per cent interval 0.17 to 0.97) and slightly better memory over time; the overall spread of memory-and-thinking diagnoses did not differ between groups. The authors say the estimates are imprecise because few people developed dementia. Not in data/.
missing.why: Dementia is one of the diseases the test names, the people had no diabetes when assigned, and the comparison is with placebo, so if it passes peer review someone will argue it meets the first-human test. On a plain reading it does not yet: it is a preprint, the test says peer-reviewed, the result is on odds of dementia at one look rather than time to a first disease, the trial was not designed to detect it, and the wide interval nearly touches no effect.

missing.what: The veterans' health service trial named in the correction above (VA-IMPACT, NCT02915198): metformin against placebo in an estimated 7,410 veterans with prediabetes and existing artery disease, started 2023-04-03, recruiting, average follow-up 4.5 years, main results expected 2029-09-28 (registry entry last updated 2025-12-17). A Swedish trial of the same kind after a heart attack (MIMET, NCT05182970, 5,160 people planned) is also registered, but its entry has not been updated since 2024-04-02 and its status is now listed as unknown. Neither is in data/.
missing.why: If it reads out on time and positive, a peer-reviewed report around 2030 would meet the first-human test (people without diabetes, placebo, death and heart disease) three years before the entry's earliest year of 2033, which assumes TAME. It has no result yet, and its people already have artery disease, so whether a delay in a further heart event counts as 'a first age-related disease' is a question for the entry's owner.

missing.what: A controlled trial of metformin to prevent Alzheimer's dementia in people without diabetes has finished its treatment phase (the MAP trial, Columbia University, NCT04098666): 326 overweight people aged 55 to 90 with early memory impairment, 18 months, a memory test as the main measure. The registry gives the main completion date as 2026-04-23 and the status as active, not recruiting; no results are posted. Not in data/.
missing.why: Results could come within a year. Its main measure is a memory score, not time to dementia, so even a positive result would bear on the reasoning more than meet the test.

missing.what: Two controlled trials of metformin in older people without a diabetes requirement reported no gain in physical function. In England (MET-PREVENT; Witham and colleagues, Lancet Healthy Longevity, 2025-03-24): 72 people of mean age 80 with weak muscles and frailty; walking speed after four months was the same as on placebo (0.57 against 0.58 metres a second), and hospital admissions were more frequent on metformin (12 of 35 against 3 of 36). In the United States (DEMFOS; Lancet Healthy Longevity, 2026-07-30): 114 adults aged 65 to 85 with obesity; adding metformin to a diet-and-exercise programme gave no further gain in physical function. Not in data/.
missing.why: Neither measures disease or death, so the test is untouched. Both tested metformin as a drug against ageing in the age group TAME would enrol and found nothing, and one found it poorly tolerated at 80, which weakens the case that a positive read-out follows once a trial runs.

missing.what: Results were posted on the registry for a placebo-controlled trial designed around metformin and ageing in people without diabetes (the ANTHEM study, Oklahoma Medical Research Foundation and University of Wisconsin, NCT04264897; results first posted 2026-07-02): 166 adults aged 40 to 75 free of chronic disease consented and 101 finished 12 weeks. Neither main measure (the body's response to insulin, and muscle mitochondrial function) showed a significant effect of treatment (P = 0.576 and 0.88 in the posted analyses). No paper of the results turned up. Not in data/.
missing.why: A short trial of body chemistry, not of disease, so it cannot meet the test. It is a completed, publicly funded trial built on the same idea as TAME and it shows the idea is being tested in pieces while TAME waits.

missing.what: A review in Ageing Research Reviews (Keys and colleagues, 2025-06-27), titled 'Emerging uncertainty on the anti-aging potential of metformin', sets out the limits of the early medical-records studies the description relies on, the attempts to repeat them, and the trials in people without diabetes, and concludes the case has weakened. Not in data/.
missing.why: The description gives the records studies of the 2010s as the human case for the drug and says nothing of the later work that failed to repeat them. The estimate already calls a positive result 'less than certain'; this is a published reason to say so more firmly.

checked: Martin-Montalvo and colleagues, Nature Communications, 2013 (https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms3192): National Institute on Aging group, low dose from middle age, longer life in mice confirmed from the abstract (see the correction on 'male').
The TAME trial: no registry entry by title, short name or sponsor on 2026-11-09, as the entry says; the sponsor's page still answers 'not found'.
The Oklahoma trial's registry entry (NCT04264897): completed 2025-03-12, 166 enrolled, results posted 2026-07-02, last updated 2026-11-05.
The registry entry of the long prevention trial's follow-up study (NCT00038727): listed as completed, 2,779 people, last updated 2026-07-30.
queries: ClinicalTrials.gov: Targeting Aging with Metformin; TAME metformin aging; American Federation for Aging Research; metformin AND aging AND (multimorbidity OR healthspan OR longevity); metformin as the treatment, with prediabetes OR aging OR dementia OR mild cognitive impairment OR frailty as the condition, 300 or more people

Europe PMC: TITLE:metformin AND TITLE:(aging OR ageing OR longevity OR healthspan OR TAME) AND (trial OR randomized) from 2025-01-01; TITLE:metformin AND (Diabetes Prevention Program OR prediabetes OR without diabetes OR non-diabetic) AND (mortality OR cardiovascular OR cancer OR dementia OR long-term OR outcomes) in the title, from 2021-01-01; TITLE:metformin, randomised trials, with dementia, cognition, cardiovascular events, frailty, older adults, macular, cancer incidence, sarcopenia or muscle in the title, from 2025-01-01

Web: TAME trial metformin aging funding launch 2026; 'Targeting Aging with Metformin' OR 'TAME trial' AFAR announcement funding secured OR enrolling (limited to afar.org, the release wires, statnews.com, nih.gov)
records.could_not_check: The NPR article of 2024-04-22 that the entry cites for 3,000 people, 5 million dollars and 45 to 70 million dollars timed out and was not re-read. The 2016 design paper's figures (three thousand people, six years) were not re-opened; the site's own log holds them. All papers were read as abstracts. Two of the three long-trial reports (deaths, 2021; heart events, 2022) predate the 2025-01-01 start of this check and are reported because the 2025 cancer report belongs with them. A conference abstract of 2025-12-01 on the same trial and the number of illnesses per person (Innovation in Aging) was seen by title only. No regulator has approved metformin to delay age-related disease; that was covered by web search only.

records.name: Fresh mitochondria are transplanted into a person's failing tissue

corrections.entry_says: Stage reached '2017-07' (the first report in children).
corrections.source_says: Europe PMC gives the paper's first publication, online, as 2017-02-15; July 2017 is the date of the printed issue. If the site dates a stage by first publication, the date is five months early in the record.

corrections.entry_says: Transplantation 'has been registered or reported in stroke (University of Washington, registry entry NCT04998357, recruiting)'.
corrections.source_says: The stroke trial has reported, which the entry does not say. Its first results were published in the Journal of Cerebral Blood Flow and Metabolism on 2024-12-04 (Walker and colleagues): no significant harm from the procedure, safety comparable to matched patients who did not have it, and the first use in the human brain; it reports safety, not improved function. The registry still lists the trial as recruiting, with 20 people planned, but its stated main completion date (2026-04-29) has passed and the entry was last updated on 2025-05-21, so 'recruiting' may be out of date. The weekly readings in data/scans mention the 2024 report; the treatment's own entry does not.

corrections.entry_says: The muscle-disease report (nine people in Korea, 2025-01-31) is listed without its finding.
corrections.source_says: The abstract says the nine adults had no severe adverse drug reactions and 'at least minimal improvement' on a standard score of the disease against their own starting point; there was no comparison group. The mitochondria came from donated umbilical-cord cells, not from the patients themselves, which makes it the first report in people of mitochondria from a donor. The registry entry (NCT04976140) agrees: completed, 9 people.

missing.what: The first placebo-controlled, double-blind trial of transplanted mitochondria with a function as its main measure was registered: 36 people in South Korea with a muscle disease that has not responded to treatment (polymyositis or dermatomyositis), one dose of donor mitochondria (PN-101, Paean Biotechnology) or placebo, main measure a standard improvement score at 12 weeks, main results expected April 2027 (NCT07122648, first posted 2025-08-14, listed as not yet recruiting and not updated since). Not found in data/.
missing.why: The estimate's likely year assumes a positive controlled result 'in heart surgery or stroke' around 2033. This is a company-run, mid-stage controlled trial in a third setting with a read-out due in 2027, six years sooner, and a company with a product is the usual route to an approval. It has not started recruiting on the registry's account, so it moves nothing yet.

missing.what: Published first results of the stroke trial (see the second correction): safety and feasibility in people having a clot removed from a brain artery, with no report of improved function.
missing.why: It is a second tissue (the brain) in which the procedure has been done in people and reported in a journal. It reports safety only, so it adds nothing to the first-human test, which is already met, and does not bear on the clinic rung.

missing.what: A neighbouring line of work the entry does not mention: an Israeli company, Minovia Therapeutics, has trials registered in which a patient's own blood-forming cells are loaded with donor mitochondria and given back, in a rare childhood disease (NCT06017869, 6 people, recruiting, updated 2026-10-13) and in a blood disorder of older age, low-risk myelodysplastic syndrome (NCT06465160, 15 people, recruiting, main results expected December 2026). An earlier trial of the same company was withdrawn with no one recruited (NCT04548843). The weekly readings in data/scans mention early findings from five patients; the entry does not.
missing.why: The blood disorder is an age-related condition, which is the entry's stated interest ('whether the same could refresh an old person's tissues'). Whether cells loaded with mitochondria count as 'an infusion or injection of mitochondria' under the test is a question of the entry's scope, not of fact, so it is flagged and not counted.

checked: Registry entry NCT02851758 (Boston Children's Hospital): recruiting, 16 people planned, main completion June 2027, last updated 2026-01-05; the entry is right.
Registry entry NCT04998357 (University of Washington): listed as recruiting, as the entry says (see the correction on how current that is).
Registry entry NCT04976140 (Paean Biotechnology, Korea): completed, 9 people; the entry is right.

Baharvand and colleagues, International Journal of Cardiology, 2024-06-04 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijcard.2024.132227): randomised, triple-blind, 30 people with a heart attack (15 given mitochondria, 15 given standard care), slightly greater gain in the heart's pumping fraction and a significant gain in exercise capacity within 40 days, and the authors' call for larger and longer studies, all as the entry says.

Emani and colleagues, 2017 (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jtcvs.2017.02.018): authors, journal and title confirmed in Europe PMC, which holds no abstract for it; the five children and four coming off support were not re-read.
No regulator's approval of mitochondrial transplantation for any condition turned up in the registry, Europe PMC or a web search.
queries: ClinicalTrials.gov: 'mitochondrial transplantation' OR 'mitochondria transplantation' OR 'mitochondrial transfer' OR 'autologous mitochondria' OR 'allogeneic mitochondria' OR PN-101 OR MNV-201 OR 'mitochondrial augmentation' (17 entries, all read; the fertility entries were set aside, as the entry's notes exclude them)

Europe PMC from 2025-01-01: titles with mitochondrial transplantation, transfer, augmentation or transplant together with patients, first-in-human, clinical trial, case report or children, reviews excluded (98 results read by title); a narrower repeat excluding animal, cell and cancer studies (20 results)
Web: mitochondrial transplantation patients clinical trial results 2026 first-in-human stroke OR heart OR 'cardiac surgery' published
pages_opened: https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=... (listing with status, size and dates for NCT04998357, NCT02851758, NCT04976140, NCT06017869, NCT06465160, NCT04548843)

Europe PMC abstracts: DOI 10.1016/j.ijcard.2024.132227, DOI 10.1016/j.ard.2024.11.005, PMCID PMC11615905 (https://doi.org/10.1177/0271678x241305230), and the record for DOI 10.1016/j.jtcvs.2017.02.018
records.could_not_check: Papers were read as abstracts. The company reports the web search summarised (results in children with a rare disease, and early findings in five patients with the blood disorder, presented at a meeting in December 2025) were not opened and are not reported as facts. The August 2026 preprint on mitochondria injected into a patient's eyes, which the weekly reading of 2026-11-01 logged, did not come up in these searches and was not re-opened. No report of the Boston children's trial beyond the 2017 paper was looked for before 2025. Regulators outside the United States were covered by web search only, which returned no approval of this kind of treatment; Japan's conditional approvals of 2026-03-06, which the brief mentions, were not looked up for this record.

records.name: A rapamycin-type drug improves an age-related measure in older people

corrections.entry_says: 'a crowd-funded year-long trial of low-dose rapamycin in 114 adults, published in 2025'.
corrections.source_says: 114 is the number who finished. The registry entry for the trial (NCT04488601) lists 129 enrolled, and the site's own publications log (moel-2025) gives 114 completers plus 11 who dropped out. 'In 114 adults' reads as the trial's size.

corrections.entry_says: Estimate: 'The 2019 failure cost the field its one company sponsor; the trials now running are academic and small.'
corrections.source_says: A company sponsor is back, with public money. On 2026-02-24 the United States agency ARPA-H named Cambrian BioPharma among seven teams sharing up to 144 million dollars, to test a new relative of rapamycin taken daily by mouth. No registry entry for that trial was found on 2026-11-09. The same announcement named rapamycin as one of three drugs in the San Antonio trial, but that trial's registry entry of 2026-11-06 (NCT07923630) lists only the other two.

missing.what: A placebo-controlled trial of weekly rapamycin in older people reported, and the result leaned against the drug (RAPA-EX-01; Stanfield and colleagues, Journal of Cachexia, Sarcopenia and Muscle, April 2026). 40 inactive adults aged 65 to 85 did a home exercise programme for 13 weeks with weekly rapamycin or placebo. On the pre-stated main measure, the number of times a person can rise from a chair in 30 seconds, the rapamycin group gained 2.13 fewer than placebo (95 per cent interval minus 4.61 to plus 0.34, P = 0.089); two planned further analyses favoured placebo and were statistically significant. Walking distance and grip strength also leaned to placebo without reaching significance. The weekly readings in data/scans mention this trial as showing no clear gain; the entry does not mention it, and neither gives the direction.
missing.why: The likely year assumes a controlled trial 'in the immune system, muscle or the gums' reports positive in the early 2030s. This is the muscle trial, in exactly the people and at the kind of dose the test describes, and it suggests the drug may blunt the gain from exercise. With the 2025 year-long trial, that is two controlled trials in a row that missed their main measure.

missing.what: The largest academic trial of a rapamycin-type drug for ageing has finished and not yet reported: the University of Wisconsin's trial of everolimus (NCT05835999, titled 'Clinical Evaluation of mTORC1 Inhibition for Geroprotection'), 106 people aged up to 80, 24 weeks, main measure the body's response to insulin. The registry gives the main completion date as 2026-06-30 and the status as completed (last updated 2026-09-04); no results are posted. The weekly reading of 2026-10-17 listed this trial as running; its completion is not in data/.
missing.why: A result is likely within a year or so, sooner than the 'early 2030s' the estimate assumes for the next mid-sized trial. Whether its main measure, a response to insulin in adults of any age from 18, counts as 'an age-related measure' in older people under the test would need a ruling if it is positive.

missing.what: A preprint from a British group (Kell and colleagues, bioRxiv, 2025-08-19) reports a placebo-controlled trial of low-dose rapamycin in older adults in which a marker of damaged, ageing immune cells (the protein p21) was significantly lower in the rapamycin group than in the placebo group. The abstract gives no numbers of people. Not found in data/.
missing.why: It is a controlled result in older people on the immune system, the same system as the 2014 trial, but it is a preprint, the measure is a cell marker and not an immune response, and the abstract does not say it was the pre-stated main measure. It does not meet the test; it is the only new controlled human finding in the drug's favour.

missing.what: Two further human studies are finished or reported without a controlled result: a Columbia University trial of rapamycin and the ageing of the ovaries in 50 women aged 35 to 45 passed its main completion date on 2025-10-21 with no results posted (NCT05836025, last updated 2025-12-26); and a Swedish pilot of rapamycin in early Alzheimer's disease, six months with no placebo group, was reported in a preprint on 2025-12-09 (Svensson and colleagues; registry entry NCT06022068, 14 people, completed). Neither is in the entry.
missing.why: Neither can meet the test: one is in women under 46 and has not reported, the other has no placebo group. They show the estimate's list of settings where trials are running (immune system, muscle, gums) is incomplete.

missing.what: A study of United States transplant records in GeroScience (Stewart and Fitzsimmons, 2026-11-05) found no meaningful difference in age at death between 4,885 kidney transplant recipients prescribed rapamycin and 6,589 who were not (64.6 against 64.3 years after adjustment). It belongs with the entry on living longer in good health and is reported there; it is noted here because this entry's notes point to that one for the lifespan question.
missing.why: A records study at transplant doses, so outside this entry's test (a dose given for ageing, a controlled trial). No effect on this entry's years.

checked: Mannick and colleagues, Science Translational Medicine, 2014-12-24 (https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.3009892): everolimus (RAD001) in elderly volunteers improved the response to flu vaccine 'by about 20%', as the entry says; the 218 people and six weeks are not in the abstract and were not re-read.

Chen and colleagues, Science Signaling, 2009-11-24 (https://doi.org/10.1126/scisignal.2000559): in old mice rapamycin restored blood-forming stem cells and enabled effective vaccination against a lethal flu infection, as the entry says (the abstract adds that it also lengthened their lives).

The 2019 failure: registry entry NCT04668352 (resTORbio, RTB101, people aged 65 and over, winter chest infections) is completed with 1,024 people and results posted 2021-06-23; a companion entry NCT04139915 was withdrawn with the stated reason that the first late-stage trial 'did not meet its primary endpoint'. The entry is right.
The 2025 year-long trial (Moel and colleagues, Aging, 2025-04-04): published in 2025; main measure and result as the site's own log gives them (not re-read in full).
No approval of a rapamycin-type drug for an age-related condition in healthy older people, and no clinic's published routine practice, turned up in any search.

records.could_not_check: The estimate says several trials are running in the gums; a registry search for rapamycin-type drugs with gum disease returned no such trial, so that statement could not be confirmed and may need a source.
